seasonReviews.outcome: You finished 5th of 6 in the round robin and missed the playoffs. Your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: A coherent five-Pokémon core carried me to the two wins I was supposed to get (2-0 over Shadow Cabinet, 2-1 over 3rd-place Cotton-Eyed), but I was shut out 0-2 in all three losses to finish 5th. The season was decided less by that core than by a failed window gamble and a registration error that benched my own answer.
seasonReviews.didWell: The draft core — Mega Floette wincon, Garchomp Steel-breaker, Talonflame Tailwind, Rotom-Wash pivot, Aegislash flex wall — was sound, was registered almost every week, and delivered the clean 2-0 over Shadow Cabinet (two Shadow-Tag-proof Ghosts plus Rotom-Wash executing Gyarados) and the 2-1 upset of a Cotton-Eyed team that finished 3rd. My window diagnosis was also genuinely correct: Serperior's Contrary Leaf Storm is a verified guaranteed OHKO on Swift Swim Mega Swampert (115%+ minimum roll), and it does learn Glare and Taunt, so the rain-hole read was real. Credit too for the week-2 plan where Spiritomb and Aegislash fully walled Mega Gengar.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The Serperior swap was a one-matchup gamble that failed its only job — despite the verified Swampert OHKO I still lost 0-2 to Golden Gate because the six killed the rain but had no durable Archaludon answer, leaning on physical Earthquake and Flare Blitz that feed its Stamina while my own notes flagged Manectric as a poor check. Worse, in week 5 I registered six without Spiritomb — the exact Ghost/Dark mon I kept at the window to hard-wall Farigiraf (immune to both its Normal and Psychic STABs) — and got swept 0-2 by Heel Turn. The support benching was chronic across the year: Wyrdeer and Absol were never registered once, and all three losses were shutouts.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: Register Spiritomb in week 5 over Overqwil to actually wall Farigiraf instead of benching the Pokémon the window decision was built on. Against Golden Gate, stop feeding Archaludon's Stamina with physical Earthquake/Flare Blitz and bring special-side Ground/Fighting pressure, dropping Manectric (my own notes called it a poor Archaludon answer) for a real check. At the draft, replace the never-used Absol with a functional sixth so the tail isn't dead weight in three 0-2 losses.

seasonReviews.outcome: You finished 6th of 6 in the round robin and missed the playoffs. Your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: A season defined by an 18-point Mega Gengar that couldn't be brought effectively in two of three pre-window weeks, followed by a correct but belated free-agency pivot that still left roster holes in the final two series. The only win came in week 3 against Heel Turn, where Skeledirge delivered exactly as drafted; everything else was a mix of draft failure, registration errors, and uncovered matchups.
seasonReviews.didWell: Skeledirge at 5 points was the best value pick on the roster — Unaware shut down Sneasler's Swords Dance and Torch Song snowballed into the week 3 win exactly as the draft reasoning predicted. The free-agency swap from Mega Gengar to Mega Metagross was the correct diagnosis: Gengar's 200 Speed was too slow for rain and its Shadow Tag was nullified by Spiritomb, and Metagross's 80/150/110 bulk with Tough Claws Bullet Punch gave the team a Mega that could actually survive a hit. Greninja at 7 and Toxapex at 8 were both solid value picks that filled their roles whenever registered. The week 3 prep was excellent — correctly identifying Skeledirge as mandatory and Gyarados Taunt as the Farigiraf answer produced the only series win.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: Spending 18 of 100 draft points on Mega Gengar was the season's fatal decision: at 200 Spe it was outsped by Mega Swampert in rain and Heliolisk, Shadow Tag was hard-walled by Spiritomb in week 2, and its frailty meant it needed screen support the roster couldn't reliably provide. In week 1, Toxapex was identified in the prep notes as 'the single best answer' to the rain matchup yet was not registered — that's a registration failure that cost a must-win series. In week 4, the prep notes explicitly stated 'Corviknight is a liability here' and 'Mirror Armor triggers Competitive Milotic via Icy Wind bounce — avoid this pairing entirely,' yet Corviknight was registered anyway, handing Milotic free Competitive boosts. The final roster had no reliable sleep counterplay for the sun matchup — no Safety Goggles, no bulky Taunt user that could survive Venusaur's Chlorophyll-boosted Sleep Powder — and Klefki was correctly identified as too fragile to guarantee Safeguard, yet was still the plan.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: Draft Mega Metagross instead of Mega Gengar from the start — it costs 17 instead of 18, provides the bulk and priority the team needed all season, and frees the Gengar slot's 18 points from being dead weight in two of the first three weeks. Register Toxapex in week 1 against Golden Gate — the prep notes already identified it as the best rain answer, and leaving it on the bench while bringing Conkeldurr (flagged as unbringable) was an avoidable loss. Do not register Corviknight in week 4 against Cotton-Eyed Pranksters — the prep notes already flagged the Competitive Milotic interaction, and Greninja or Reuniclus should have taken that slot. Find a Safety Goggles user or a bulkier Taunt pivot before week 5 — the sun matchup was lost because the roster had no reliable answer to Chlorophyll Sleep Powder, and relying on Klefki Safeguard when the notes already said it was too fragile was not a plan.

seasonReviews.outcome: You reached the playoffs as the 4th seed and were eliminated in the semifinals. Your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: A 2-3 round-robin season that scraped into the playoffs as the 4th seed and was eliminated 0-2 in the first playoff round — a season defined by never solving the Golden Gate rain core, which beat me 0-2 twice including the elimination, while the window's headline fix (Venusaur-Mega) failed to actually solve it.
seasonReviews.didWell: The draft built a genuinely flexible, well-reasoned core — Incineroar's Intimidate pivot, Sneasler's Unburden anchor, Farigiraf's Armor Tail, and Gardevoir-Mega's Pixilate nuke — and the window swaps were conceptually sound: Venusaur-Mega for the rain/Swampert problem and Weavile for the Skeledirge/Gyarados problem. I beat Drought Dodgers and Fairy Tails convincingly (2-1, 2-0), and my prep notes repeatedly nailed opponent tendencies (Milotic Competitive, Corviknight Mirror Armor, Arcanine Shuca, Tsareena Queenly Majesty), which is why the two wins were clean.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The season's defining failure was the Golden Gate rain core, which I lost 0-2 to twice, including the playoff elimination — and the window's headline fix didn't work: Venusaur-Mega is 2x Ice-weak (only neutral with Thick Fat), gets outsped by Swift Swim Swampert, and my own week-2 note demanded 'two independent checks to Mega Swampert, one not OHKO-able by Ice Punch,' which Venusaur-Mega never was. The week-3 Shadow Cabinet loss to Skeledirge was a registration gap my own note flagged ('bring a Taunt-proof Trick Room setter') but the registered six didn't cover. I also leaned too heavily on Sneasler as the only fast offensive anchor, so when it couldn't get going the team had no second gear.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: At the window I'd have prioritized a genuine, non-Ice-weak Swampert check over the Skeledirge check, since Golden Gate was the team that beat me twice — Venusaur-Mega was a flawed answer and the playoff rematch proved it. I'd register a Taunt-proof or faster Trick Room setter for the Skeledirge/Gyarados matchup instead of relying on Farigiraf's Mental Herb. I'd add a second fast offensive anchor so the team doesn't collapse when Sneasler is pressured or sashed early. And I'd stop claiming Venusaur-Mega 'resists Ice' — it's 2x weak, only neutral with Thick Fat, which is exactly the kind of factual error that cost the playoff series.

seasonReviews.outcome: You reached the playoffs as the 3rd seed and were eliminated in the semifinals. Your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: We reached the semifinals as the third seed, but the season was defined by a strong early core and an increasingly exploitable lack of immediate offensive pressure. The decisive failures were the 1-2 loss to Fairy Tails, the 0-2 loss to Golden Gate Archaludons, and the playoff rematch against Drought Dodgers.
seasonReviews.didWell: Whimsicott, Gholdengo, Milotic, and Arcanine were a sound foundation, and the 2-1 wins over Heel Turn and Drought showed that the original roster could execute strong Tailwind, Competitive, sand, rain, and Fire-pressure plans. The week-two Arcanine set and the week-four Sinistcha/Grimmsnarl registration were particularly good matchup-specific calls; Sinistcha's Rage Powder and Strength Sap helped beat Shadow Cabinet's physical and Ground pressure. We also correctly preserved Milotic against Intimidate and used Prankster Encore, Taunt, and Tailwind as real tempo tools rather than treating Whimsicott as passive support.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The draft spent 19 points on Whimsicott and 16 on Gholdengo while filling the back half with several one- and two-point utility picks, leaving too little reliable damage once a matchup invalidated the main attackers. At the window, dropping Basculegion-Male for Sinistcha removed the roster's best immediate Water pressure, and replacing Mega Tyranitar with Grimmsnarl solved weather conflict but left us without a powerful Mega attacker; the Fairy Tails and Archaludon losses exposed that trade. In those series we registered passive defensive structures into Rotom-Wash, Tsareena, Wide Guard, and Archaludon, then piloted around weather or screens without producing immediate target pressure; the playoff loss similarly lacked a concrete answer to Venusaur's Sleep Powder and Charizard's ability to restore sun.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: I would keep Basculegion-Male at the window and test a cheaper support swap instead of removing both it and Mega Tyranitar's offensive threat; Sinistcha's utility was valuable, but it could not replace Basculegion's damage. Against Fairy Tails, I would register a Ground- and Electric-safe offensive six with a direct Rotom-Wash answer rather than pairing Milotic and Basculegion, and I would use single-target attacks to avoid Wide Guard and Yache Berry issues. Against Golden Gate, I would prioritize immediate Archaludon damage and a tested Tsareena answer over dual screens and passive recovery. In the playoff rematch, I would lead a plan that directly pressures Venusaur or denies its sleep turns, preserve Milotic for Dragonite and weather control, and avoid relying on Heatproof Sinistcha to survive repeated Charizard attacks.

seasonReviews.outcome: You reached the final and lost it. You are the league runner-up and your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: We achieved a runner-up finish behind a 3-2 regular season and a playoff final appearance, powered by an elite Rain engine that swept every non-Sun opponent 2-0. Our season was ultimately defined and ended by an unaddressed structural weakness against Drought Dodgers' Mega Charizard Y and Chlorophyll Venusaur core.
seasonReviews.didWell: Drafting Archaludon (Pick 6), Pelipper (Pick 7), and Mega Swampert (Pick 18) alongside Tsareena (Pick 19) established an oppressive offensive engine that dictated tempo against teams like Heel Turn Incineroars and Fairy Tails. Securing Scrafty at 3 points and Garganacl at 5 points provided incredible point efficiency and Wide Guard utility that anchored our defensive setups. In piloting, Choice Scarf Queenly Majesty Tsareena consistently shut down opposing Fake Out and priority strategies to secure clean series sweeps.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: Standing pat at the free-agency window after losing Week 3 to Drought Dodgers was a critical window mistake that left our Sun matchup completely exposed. In the playoff finals, our registration decision to bench Pelipper and Mega Swampert entirely was a major registration error. That decision forced a slow Trick Room registration of Mimikyu, Armarouge, and Galarian Slowking, which was easily dismantled by Chlorophyll Venusaur's fast Sleep Powder and Mega Charizard Y's Sun-boosted attacks without active weather override.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: At the free-agency window, I would swap Heliolisk (4 pts) or Armarouge (8 pts) for a sleep-immune or weather-neutralizing pivot like Safety Goggles Dragonite to directly solve Sun offense. In registration for the finals against Drought Dodgers, I would bring Pelipper and Archaludon to actively fight for Drizzle weather control instead of abandoning our primary win condition.

seasonReviews.outcome: You won the final. You are the league champion and the season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: We finished 4-1 in the round robin, won both playoff series, and became league champion with a 9-2 game record. The season was defined by a correctly drafted and repeatedly well-registered Mega Charizard Y/Venusaur weather core, backed by enough disruption and Steel pressure to adapt after the two regular-season losses.
seasonReviews.didWell: The draft’s decisive success was taking Mega Charizard Y, Venusaur, Kingambit, Raichu, and Paldean Tauros-Aqua: that group supplied the sun tempo, Chlorophyll pressure, Fairy/Ghost punishment, Electric protection, and physical utility that won the league. The week-3 2-1 and playoff 2-0 wins over Golden Gate showed the roster’s clearest matchup advantage: Charizard overwrote Pelipper rain, Venusaur threatened Mega Swampert, and Raichu/Kingambit covered the rest of the rain and Trick Room structures. Registration improved meaningfully after the week-2 Cotton-Eyed loss: the playoff rematch correctly left Tauros out to avoid Competitive Milotic, used Charizard/Raichu to contest Whimsicott, and added Dragonite plus Sableye as independent speed-control and disruption routes. Keeping the roster unchanged at free agency was ultimately a sound window decision; the existing six- and seven-mon rotations beat every opponent, including the teams that changed their rosters.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The two regular-season losses exposed a draft-depth weakness: Altaria, Emolga, and Avalugg never became registered solutions, so three one-point selections did not materially expand the weekly tool kit. Against Cotton-Eyed in week 2, the Charizard/Venusaur plan was too dependent on preserving sun through Whimsicott Encore and the Arcanine/Gholdengo/Mega Tyranitar core; that was primarily a registration problem, not evidence that the core itself was bad. Week 4 against Heel Turn was the clearest structural bad matchup: opposing Mega Venusaur, together with Sneasler’s Rock Slide pressure, made both Tauros and Charizard uncomfortable, and no registered six converted Kingambit’s theoretical value into a stable answer. There is not enough game-by-game information to assign either series loss to a specific piloting error, but the pre-series plans correctly identified risks that the registrations did not fully solve.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: In the draft, I would spend at least one of the Altaria/Emolga/Avalugg slots on a player that can be registered regularly into bulky Grass and Rock-pressure structures, rather than carrying three specialists that never appeared. For the first Cotton-Eyed series, I would register Sableye over Venusaur or Tauros and build explicitly around Taunt/Quash plus Dragonite Tailwind, giving the team a speed-control plan that does not collapse when sun is interrupted. For the Heel Turn series, I would not lead from the assumption that Charizard Y/Venusaur is the primary mode; I would register Sableye over one of the less reliable sun pieces and make Kingambit preservation, Taunt/Quash, and Dragonite Tailwind the central anti-Mega-Venusaur plan. At the free-agency window, I would still keep the championship core, but I would have looked harder for a concrete replacement for one unused one-point slot rather than treating all three low-cost matchup options as equally valuable.

roster.name: Mega Gengar
roster.rationale: Shadow Tag is the most uniquely game-warping ability in VGC — it traps opponents, eliminates safe switching, and lets Mega Gengar's 170 SpA / 130 Spe pick off key support Pokémon at will. At 18 points it's elite value for a pick that forces every opponent to build around it, and it leaves 82 points for 9 more slots, plenty to build a complete roster.

roster.name: Corviknight
roster.rationale: Corviknight at 13 fills two critical needs in one slot — Tailwind speed control for Mega Gengar and a Steel-type defensive backbone with premium Flying/Steel typing. Mirror Armor reflects Intimidate and Snarl, it has U-turn for pivoting, and at 13 points it's excellent value, leaving 69 for 8 picks. Noivern (9) and Talonflame (15) remain as backup Tailwind options if needed later.

roster.name: Gyarados
roster.rationale: Gyarados at 11 fills two needs in one slot — Intimidate support and a strong physical attacker with Dragon Dance, Taunt, and Waterfall/Crunch coverage. It pairs excellently with Mega Gengar (Gengar traps Fairy-types that threaten Gyarados, while Gyarados provides Intimidate to protect Gengar's frailer teammates), and the Water/Flying typing complements my Corviknight + Gengar core without stacking weaknesses. At 11 points it's strong value, leaving 58 for 7 picks (8.3 avg) to address remaining needs.

roster.name: Greninja
roster.rationale: Greninja at 7 points is exceptional value for a premier special attacker — 122 Speed with Protean gives me flexible STAB coverage on everything, filling my biggest roster gap at nearly half the cost of Volcarona or Primarina. This preserves 51 points across 6 remaining picks, letting me comfortably address Prankster support, physical breaking, and the Electric weakness that Gyarados/Corviknight/Greninja all share. Water/Dark typing also adds Dark coverage my roster currently lacks.

roster.name: Mamoswine
roster.rationale: Mamoswine at 12 fills two needs in one pick: a dedicated physical wallbreaker with 130 base Attack and excellent Ice/Ground STAB coverage, plus a Ground-type that gives me an Electric immunity (3 of my 4 current mons are weak to Electric). Thick Fat also patches its Fire and Ice weaknesses, making it a durable offensive pivot. This efficiency lets me preserve picks and budget for Prankster support and utility later.

roster.name: Klefki
roster.rationale: Klefki at 11 is the best-value Prankster support on the board, giving me priority Thunder Wave, dual screens, and Swagger/Foul Play utility while adding a Steel/Fairy defensive typing that complements Gyarados and Mamoswine. At 11 points it leaves 28 for four remaining picks, keeping budget flexibility to address special wall and filler needs. Sableye (14) is arguably stronger but would over-constrain the remaining 25 points across four slots.

roster.name: Toxapex
roster.rationale: Toxapex is the premier special wall available and my biggest remaining need — Regenerator pivoting, Haze for setup counterplay against DD/SD sweepers, and Toxic Spikes chip are all unique utilities nothing else on my roster provides. With Golden Gate holding 23 pts and Fairy Tails 13 pts, both could contest this pick before it comes back to me, so securing it now at 8 pts preserves 20 for my final three slots.

roster.name: Reuniclus
roster.rationale: Reuniclus is the premier Trick Room setter my roster is missing — base 30 Speed, 125 SpA, and Magic Guard make it both a TR lead and a TR win condition that ignores hazards and weather chip. Pure Psychic typing avoids stacking a fourth Water type onto Gyarados/Greninja/Toxapex, and at 8 points it leaves 12 for my final two slots (Conkeldurr at 7 for Fighting priority, then a 4–5 cost utility pick). Golden Gate has 11 points and could contest TR setters, so grabbing it now is priority.

roster.name: Conkeldurr
roster.rationale: Conkeldurr fills the Fighting-type priority/breaker hole perfectly at 7 points, leaving exactly 5 for a utility pick next round. Mach Punch gives me priority outside of Mamoswine's Ice Shard, Guts turns status into a power boost (synergizing with TR from Reuniclus), and base 45 Speed makes it a natural Trick Room attacker. Golden Gate had 11 points and could have sniped this, so locking it now is critical.

roster.name: Skeledirge
roster.rationale: Skeledirge's Unaware is the single best setup counterplay available at 5 points, shutting down Kingambit Supreme Overlord, Dragonite DD, Archaludon Stamina boosts, and Mega Swampert rain sweeps across multiple opponents. Its Fire/Ghost typing fills a gap on my roster (no Fire-type currently) and gives me a Torch Song wincon that snowballs SpA while still functioning as a defensive pivot. This rounds out the team with a dedicated wall that complements Toxapex's Haze as a second layer of boost denial.

roster.name: Mega Charizard Y
roster.rationale: Mega Charizard Y is the premier immediate-pressure pick still available: Drought, 159 Special Attack, and Fire/Flying coverage force extensive respect while enabling multiple cheap sun shells later. It also preserves a flexible Mega slot in-game and gives us a proactive weather plan rather than trying to play directly into the Shadow Tag Gengar coach’s preferred trapping games.

roster.name: Venusaur
roster.rationale: Venusaur is the most reliable and flexible Chlorophyll partner for Mega Charizard Y, giving the roster immediate sun speed pressure, Sleep Powder disruption, and strong Water/Fairy/Grass counterplay. At 13 points it preserves enough budget to build a deep matchup-specific supporting cast rather than committing to another expensive centerpiece.

roster.name: Kingambit
roster.rationale: Kingambit is the best remaining premium glue for this start: it gives a strong Mega Gengar/Gholdengo/Mega Floette answer, punishes Incineroar Intimidate through Defiant, and supplies priority pressure with Sucker Punch. Its Fighting weakness is manageable with Mega Charizard Y and Venusaur, while its Steel typing adds valuable defensive structure to the sun core.

roster.name: Raichu
roster.rationale: Raichu gives this sun core a crucial Lightning Rod shield for Mega Charizard Y, while also providing Fake Out, Nuzzle-based speed control, and flexible disruption. At 10 points it preserves the budget needed to add several matchup-specific role players, including Ground/Rock answers and anti-Trick Room tools.

roster.name: Dragonite
roster.rationale: Dragonite gives this sun core a bulky Ground immunity, strong priority through Extreme Speed, and a physical win condition that does not overlap with Charizard Y or Venusaur’s special pressure. Multiscale also makes it a flexible anti-offense and anti-Trick Room pick, while its Flying typing helps cover the Ground pressure aimed at Raichu and Kingambit.

roster.name: Paldean Tauros Aqua
roster.rationale: At 3 points, Paldean Tauros-Aqua is exceptional value: Intimidate supplies the physical mitigation this roster lacks, while its Water/Fighting typing checks Rock-types and gives a useful rain-matchup option without committing the team to rain. It also offers flexible utility through Raging Bull, Close Combat, Aqua Jet, Chilling Water, and potentially setup or speed control.

roster.name: Sableye
roster.rationale: Sableye is the best remaining all-purpose support fit at this price: Prankster Taunt, Will-O-Wisp, Encore/Quash, screens, and Fake Out give the roster flexible answers to Trick Room, physical offense, and speed control. It also carries Imprison + Trick Room as a non-Prankster anti-TR option into Farigiraf-centered teams, where priority disruption is blocked.

roster.name: Altaria
roster.rationale: Altaria is an excellent 1-point matchup specialist: Cloud Nine can switch off the opposing Pelipper–Mega Swampert rain mode and Mega Tyranitar sand while retaining Tailwind, Haze, Helping Hand, Perish Song, and bulky disruption options. It also adds another Ground immunity and a Water resistance for teams where Charizard Y sun is not the preferred weather plan.

roster.name: Emolga
roster.rationale: Emolga is the best 1-point utility complement: Motor Drive gives a second Electric immunity while Flying supplies another Ground immunity for a roster that can otherwise be pressured by Earthquake. It offers distinct disruption through Nuzzle, Encore, Taunt, Electroweb, Speed Swap, Helping Hand, and pivoting with Volt Switch/U-turn rather than merely duplicating Raichu’s Fake Out role.

roster.name: Avalugg
roster.rationale: Avalugg supplies a distinct, inexpensive matchup slot: Sturdy plus immense physical Defense gives the roster a plausible answer into Garchomp, Mega Tyranitar, Dragonite, and other physical attackers, while its Ice coverage pressures Dragons that otherwise force heavy reliance on Kingambit. It can also function as a dedicated Wide Guard/Body Press-style utility option where spread-move protection matters.

roster.rationale: Archaludon is an elite VGC anchor, combining a fantastic Steel/Dragon typing that boasts nine resistances with centralizing abilities like Stamina and Stalwart. Its sheer physical bulk and Body Press presence punish physical attackers, while Electro Shot gives it terrifying special scaling. Drafting Archaludon as our first pick provides a versatile pillar that fits seamlessly into bulky balance, rain offense, or anti-redirection strategies.

roster.name: Pelipper
roster.rationale: Pairing Archaludon with Pelipper immediately establishes a premier Rain core, unlocking one-turn Electro Shots with instant Special Attack boosts while providing vital speed control via Tailwind and spread protection via Wide Guard. Pelipper's Drizzle eliminates Archaludon's Fire neutralities across team setups, severely pressures opposing Sun (Mega Charizard Y) and Incineroar compositions, and secures our core weather setter early.

roster.name: Mega Swampert
roster.rationale: Mega Swampert secures our premier Mega Evolution and physical Swift Swim sweeper, forming a lethal rain core alongside Pelipper and Archaludon. Its Water/Ground typing grants a vital Electric immunity to protect Pelipper, while its massive 100/110/110 bulk and 150 base Attack allow it to overpower opposing defense under Drizzle. At 15 points, it offers superior defense and stat distribution compared to other rain sweepers, leaving us with 48 points to fill our remaining 7 slots.

roster.name: Tsareena
roster.rationale: Tsareena provides essential Grass and Electric resistances to shield our Rain core, along with physical Grass STAB via Trop Kick and Power Whip. Her ability Queenly Majesty completely neutralizes opposing priority moves like Fake Out, Sucker Punch, and Gale Wings, granting clean turns for Mega Swampert and Archaludon. At 11 points, she leaves us a healthy 37 points across our final 6 picks to round out anti-Trick Room and pivot support.

roster.name: Mimikyu
roster.rationale: Mimikyu gives our Rain team an unshakeable anti-Trick Room lever and crucial ghost/fairy typing. Disguise guarantees a turn to reverse enemy Trick Room, drop Will-O-Wisp burns on physical threats, or disrupt with Taunt and Shadow Sneak. At 11 points, it adds immunity to Normal, Fighting, and Dragon moves while leaving 26 points for our final 5 picks.

roster.name: Scrafty
roster.rationale: Scrafty fills our primary structural need for Intimidate and Fake Out support at a remarkable price of 3 points. Its Dark/Fighting typing absorbs Dark and Ghost attacks aimed at Mimikyu, while providing Fake Out turn control to set up Rain or Trick Room safely. Knock Off, Snarl, and Coaching give us immense defensive and offensive utility to bolster Archaludon and Mega Swampert.

roster.name: Armarouge
roster.rationale: Armarouge simultaneously fills our two most urgent needs by providing a high-output special Fire threat to vaporize Grass-types that target Mega Swampert and supplying Wide Guard to shield our core rain sweepers from opposing spread moves. It also adds a potent secondary Trick Room setting and abusing threat that pairs seamlessly with Mimikyu for flexible speed control. Flash Fire gives us a crucial Fire immunity to pivot into, while moves like Clear Smog, Ally Switch, and Helping Hand offer rich situational utility.

roster.name: Heliolisk
roster.rationale: Heliolisk is an ideal 4-point addition to our Rain core, taking advantage of Dry Skin for passive healing and Water immunity while delivering 100% accurate Thunders and 150-effective-BP Water Weather Balls. Its base 109 Speed gives us vital fast speed control with Electroweb/Glare as well as pivoting via Volt Switch and U-turn to maintain pressure with Mega Swampert and Archaludon. Spending 4 points leaves us a healthy 11 points across our final two picks, fully preserving our ability to draft a high-impact 5- or 6-point wall next round.

roster.name: Garganacl
roster.rationale: Garganacl (5 pts) gives us an incredible defensive anchor with Purifying Salt status immunity, Wide Guard support, and Salt Cure chip damage that heavily punishes opposing Water and Steel types. It synergizes seamlessly with our Trick Room options (Mimikyu, Armarouge) while offering a physical wall that requires zero team support in rain or neutral weather. Spending 5 points leaves 6 points in our remaining budget, preserving total flexibility for our final Pick 10 flex slot.

roster.name: Galarian Slowking
roster.rationale: Galarian Slowking perfectly rounds out our 10-mon roster by providing a premier specially defensive Regenerator pivot and a crucial Poison/Psychic resistance profile against opposing Fairy and Grass threats. Access to Chilly Reception, Yawn, Eerie Impulse, and secondary Trick Room setting creates seamless pivot synergy for Mega Swampert, Archaludon, and Armarouge. With its elite 95/80/110 bulk and Regenerator, it gives us an unkillable defensive anchor against hyper-offensive special teams.

teambuilds.rationale: Whimsicott gives the team Prankster Tailwind, Encore, and Helping Hand support while Moonblast pressures Sneasler and the opposing Dark types. Gholdengo and Mega Tyranitar provide strong answers to Mega Gardevoir, Skarmory, Sinistcha, and Appletun, with Milotic punishing Intimidate through Competitive and checking Incineroar and Samurott. Arcanine supplies Intimidate, Snarl, and Will-O-Wisp utility, while Lopunny offers Fake Out and immediate Fighting-type pressure under Tailwind.

Bring the sun core to pressure Rotom-Wash, Garchomp, and Aegislash, while Venusaur’s Chlorophyll gives us immediate speed control even into Choice Scarf variants. Kingambit and Expert Belt Tauros provide two direct Fairy punishers for Mega Floette, while Raichu protects the mode from Electric pressure and Sableye disrupts Trick Room or faster threats with Prankster. Lead Charizard/Venusaur aggressively when their Fire answers are constrained; Raichu or Sableye can instead lead beside either attacker for Fake Out, Quash, or Taunt support.

Mega Charizard Y plus Venusaur is the primary pressure mode: Raichu can Fake Out Whimsicott to deny Tailwind while Charizard establishes sun, and Venusaur then outruns their entire unboosted roster. Kingambit covers Gholdengo and Chimecho while exploiting their multiple Intimidate options, whereas Tauros is the direct Mega Tyranitar answer and Dragonite supplies a bulkier secondary speed-control and priority mode. Avoid cycling Intimidate into a revealed Competitive Milotic unless the board position makes the boost irrelevant.

This six is built to contest Drought with Mega Tyranitar's Sand Stream and dual Rain Dance options, while preserving strong answers to Charizard-Y, Venusaur, Dragonite, and Kingambit. Whimsicott supplies Prankster Tailwind, Taunt, and Encore, while Milotic punishes Paldean Tauros's Intimidate with Competitive and provides Ice coverage. Flash Fire Arcanine avoids triggering Kingambit's Defiant and pressures the sun core, while Swift Swim Basculegion becomes a major rain-mode attacker.

Against Heel Turn Incineroars, our primary engine is Swift Swim Rain Offense with Mega Swampert, Pelipper, and Archaludon, which outpaces and overpowers core threats like Mega Gardevoir, Incineroar, and Sneasler under Drizzle. Queenly Majesty Tsareena blocks priority Fake Out from Incineroar and Sneasler while applying immediate Choice Scarf pressure. Garganacl invalidates Mega Gardevoir's Pixilate Hyper Voice and Sinistcha's Matcha Gotcha with Wide Guard while chipping Skarmory and Samurott via Salt Cure. Mimikyu provides safety via Disguise to reverse potential Trick Room setups and shut down support moves with Taunt.

Against The Shadow Cabinet's hyper-offensive balance, we bring a high-tempo Rain offense core backstopped by priority protection and Regenerator pivot support. Mega Swampert under Drizzle rain outspeeds Mega Gengar and OHKOs key targets like Mega Gengar, Skeledirge, and Mamoswine with High Horsepower and Liquidation. Archaludon and Life Orb Dry Skin Heliolisk abuse rain with 1-turn Electro Shot, 100% accurate Thunders, and 100 BP Water Weather Ball while gaining passive healing. Tsareena's Queenly Majesty completely neutralizes priority status and attacks from Klefki or incoming revenge killers, while Galarian Slowking provides a Regenerator wall against Conkeldurr and Toxapex.

Opponent leans on a Drizzle rain core (Pelipper + Mega Swampert Swift Swim) plus bulky physical attackers (Tsareena, Scrafty, Mimikyu, Garganacl) and special threats (Archaludon, Armarouge, Heliolisk, Galarian Slowking). My six answer each pillar: Dedenne's Electric deletes Pelipper and Nuzzles for speed control; Sinistcha's 4x Giga Drain removes Mega Swampert and Rage Powder redirects; Farigiraf's Armor Tail blocks priority (Aqua Jet/Sucker Punch/Fake Out) and Trick Room reverses Swift Swim; Incineroar's Intimidate + Fake Out + Parting Shot neuters the physical attackers; Gardevoir-Mega's Pixilate Hyper Voice nukes Scrafty/Mimikyu; Sneasler's Unburden Close Combat breaks Archaludon, Garganacl, and Heliolisk. Note Tsareena's Queenly Majesty blocks my priority, so I lean on Trick Room and speed control rather than Fake Out when she's active.

The opponent leans heavily physical (Mega Tyranitar, Arcanine, Tauros, Lopunny, Furfrou, Basculegion) with a few special threats (Gholdengo, Milotic, Chimecho, Whimsicott). Incineroar's Intimidate + Will-O-Wisp + Fake Out + Parting Shot neutralizes the physical core, while Sneasler (Focus Sash + Unburden) cleanly OHKOs Mega Tyranitar, Tauros, Lopunny, and even Furfrou through Fur Coat with Close Combat, and hits Gholdengo with Shadow Claw. Gardevoir-Mega's Pixilate Hyper Voice pressures Tyranitar and its Shadow Ball threatens Gholdengo. Sinistcha redirects attacks with Rage Powder, heals with Strength Sap, and hits Basculegion/Milotic with Matcha Gotcha. Dedenne (Choice Scarf) answers Basculegion and Milotic with Thunderbolt, and Skarmory sets Tailwind and walls physical attackers with Body Press.

This six answers the opponent's triple threat of Mega Floette (155 SpA), Garchomp (130 Atk), and Talonflame (Gale Wings priority). Corviknight and Toxapex form an unbreakable Fairy wall core — both take under 44% from Moonblast while Corviknight is immune to Garchomp EQ. Mamoswine provides priority Ice Shard to revenge Garchomp (52-118%) and Rock Slide to punish Talonflame (67-162%). Mega Gengar traps and removes key targets post-Mega Evolution: Thunderbolt for Talonflame, Shadow Ball for Aegislash/Spiritomb, Sludge Bomb for Mega Floette. Gyarados Intimidate drops Garchomp's Outrage to non-OHKO range and Taunt shuts Spiritomb Trick Room. Klefki's Prankster Thunder Wave and Reflect provide speed control and physical bulk insurance.

Drought Dodgers run the Mega Charizard Y sun core with Chlorophyll Venusaur, plus Kingambit, Dragonite, and Paldean Tauros as physical threats. Rotom-Wash and Garchomp's Rock Slide answer Charizard, Aegislash's Wide Guard shuts off sun Heat Wave and Sludge Wave, and Talonflame turns their own sun into a weapon with Flare Blitz while setting Tailwind. Mega Floette is the win condition: Fairy Aura Moonblast OHKOs Dragonite through Multiscale, Altaria, Tauros, and Sableye, and Calm Mind lets it sweep once Kingambit is burned or removed. Spiritomb provides a Fighting immunity, Prankster immunity, and Pressure PP drain in a 20-PP format.

The opponent's rain core (Pelipper + Swift Swim Mega Swampert) is the primary threat. Mega Gengar's Thunderbolt guarantees a OHKO on Pelipper (4x), instantly removing rain; Gyarados (Intimidate, resists Water, immune to Ground) is the primary Mega Swampert switch-in. Klefki's Prankster Thunder Wave provides priority speed control — paralyzing Mega Swampert drops it to 134 effective speed (Swift Swim 2x × paralysis 0.5x), which Jolly Gyarados at 146 outspeeds. Corviknight sets Tailwind for broader speed control and runs a specially bulky Careful spread that survives Armarouge Flamethrower and Heliolisk Thunderbolt (both possible OHKOs on a physical spread). Mamoswine's Earthquake hits Archaludon/Armarouge/Heliolisk super effectively and Ice Shard adds priority cleanup. Conkeldurr's Close Combat threatens possible OHKOs on Archaludon and Garganacl, Mach Punch adds priority, and Guts makes it a status absorber.

Their core is Mega Gengar's Shadow Tag plus heavy physical attackers (Mamoswine, Conkeldurr, Gyarados) and fast Greninja, so I bring two Ghosts that Shadow Tag can't hold: Spiritomb walls Gengar (Shadow Ball immune, Sludge Bomb ~25%, Dazzling Gleam maxes at 65%) and Sucker Punches it back, while Aegislash Wide Guards the spread Poison/Fairy spam and Shadow Balls Gengar and Reuniclus. Rotom-Wash is the Gyarados executioner (guaranteed Thunderbolt OHKO) and Mamoswine wall (EQ immune, Ice resisted, Hydro Pump 80-189%), and Talonflame sets Tailwind at 195 Speed to edge max Greninja while Quick Guard shelters Garchomp from Ice Shard and Mach Punch. Under Tailwind, Mega Floette outspeeds everything and Fairy Aura Moonblast OHKOes Greninja (134%+) and Conkeldurr (119%+), with Psychic answering Gengar and Toxapex after Calm Mind. Garchomp cleans up with Life Orb Earthquake once their Ice users are down.

This six answers Heel Turn's fast physical core (Sneasler/Incineroar) and special nuke (Mega Gardevoir) with layered counterplay. Skeledirge hard-walls Sneasler (immune to Fighting, resists Poison, Unaware ignores Swords Dance) while Torch Song snowballs and 2HKOs Skarmory/Sinistcha. Mega Gengar at 200 Spe outspeeds and threatens OHKO on Gardevoir with Shadow Ball or Sludge Bomb, then Shadow Tag traps to eliminate key targets. Corviknight + Klefki form a Steel backbone that resists Gardevoir's Pixilate Hyper Voice (12-50%), while Corviknight's Mirror Armor reflects the opponent's Intimidate and Tailwind gives the team speed control (reaching 190 Spe, outspeeding Jolly Sneasler). Gyarados provides a second Intimidate to neuter physical attackers, Taunt to shut down Farigiraf's Trick Room, and Waterfall to threaten Incineroar. Mamoswine with Focus Sash is the emergency speed control (Ice Shard priority) and ground coverage (High Horsepower for Incineroar/Alakazam). Klefki sets dual screens with Light Clay and Prankster Thunder Wave for speed control when Armor Tail isn't active.

The Shadow Cabinet leans on Mega Gengar's Shadow Tag trap plus fast Water/Dark and physical Fighting/Ice pressure. Sneasler naturally outspeeds Mega Gengar and removes it (and Reuniclus/Skeledirge) with super-effective Throat Chop, while Farigiraf's Armor Tail shuts down Greninja/Conkeldurr/Mamoswine priority and gives Trick Room speed control. Dedenne is the dedicated Gyarados/Greninja answer with 4x Thunderbolt and Nuzzle paralysis, backed by Incineroar's Intimidate pivot and Skarmory's Tailwind + physical walling. Gardevoir-Mega's Pixilate Hyper Voice cleans up Conkeldurr, Mamoswine, and Toxapex. I keep Gardevoir and Farigiraf shielded from Ghost attacks while Sneasler and Incineroar's Dark moves remove the Ghost threats first.

Whimsicott provides Prankster Tailwind and Encore while Mega Tyranitar, Gholdengo, and Basculegion apply immediate spread and single-target pressure into Floette, Talonflame, Garchomp, and Aegislash. Milotic is the primary Garchomp and weather check with Ice Beam and bulky recovery, while Arcanine adds Intimidate, Snarl, and Fire coverage against the Steel- and Ghost-heavy roster. The six use distinct items and preserve both fast Tailwind offense and defensive counterplay to opposing physical and special modes.

Mega Charizard Y is the weather-control centerpiece: it overwrites Pelipper rain, denies Mega Swampert's Swift Swim, and pairs with Chlorophyll Venusaur to threaten immediate Grass KOs. Raichu provides the crucial Heliolisk/Electric answer and speed disruption, while Tauros, Kingambit, and Sableye cover the physical rain core, Psychic/Fairy pieces, Intimidate cycling, and Trick Room options. Avoid leading priority disruption into Tsareena; use Charizard's Fire/Flying pressure to remove it first.

This composition counters the opponent's Drought/Sun offense centered around Mega Charizard Y and Chlorophyll Venusaur. Queenly Majesty Tsareena completely shuts down opposing priority options (Raichu's Fake Out, Dragonite's Extreme Speed, Kingambit's Sucker Punch, and Sableye's Prankster status moves), allowing our aggressive Rain engine to operate unhindered. Pelipper and Galarian Slowking (via Chilly Reception) maintain weather control to strip Chlorophyll speed and halve Fire damage. Under Rain, Swift Swim Mega Swampert and Wise Glasses Archaludon easily break through their remaining pieces with boosted Water attacks and instant +1 SpA Electro Shots, while Garganacl offers Wide Guard support against Heat Wave.

They will likely bring Whimsicott, Gholdengo, Mega Tyranitar, Basculegion, Milotic and Arcanine/Tauros, so this six stacks answers to each pillar: Overqwil Intimidates every physical threat and guaranteed-OHKOs Whimsicott with Poison Jab, Talonflame sets Tailwind and Quick Guards Prankster priority, Yache Garchomp Earthquakes Gholdengo/Tyranitar/Arcanine while surviving one Ice Beam, and Rotom-Wash walls Arcanine and Basculegion while Hydro Pumping Tyranitar. Aegislash Wide Guards Rock Slide/Earthquake/Make It Rain and eats Normal/Psychic hits, and Mega Floette is the cleaner: Fairy Aura Light of Ruin is an OHKO roll on Mega Tyranitar and Energy Ball deletes their Waters. Lead Overqwil + Talonflame into Whimsicott leads, Rotom-Wash + Garchomp into Tyranitar/Arcanine, and keep Floette out of Gholdengo.

Whimsicott provides immediate Prankster Tailwind, Taunt, and Encore to pressure opposing speed control and Trick Room attempts, while Milotic punishes Intimidate from Gyarados and Arcanine with Competitive. Gholdengo and Charcoal Arcanine supply strong spread pressure into Klefki, Corviknight, and Mega Metagross; Sinistcha redirects attacks and restores team health, while Grimmsnarl adds screens and Parting Shot for the physical-heavy matchup.

Whimsicott provides priority Tailwind, Taunt, and Encore to disrupt rain offense and Trick Room attempts, while Gholdengo and Milotic pressure Archaludon, Pelipper, Mega Swampert, and Mimikyu from the special side. Sinistcha offers Rage Powder, Strength Sap, and Grass damage into the Water/Ground core, with Hospitality and Sitrus Berry improving its longevity. Grimmsnarl supplies dual screens and Parting Shot, while Intimidate Tauros adds fast Fighting and Rock pressure against Archaludon, Scrafty, and Pelipper.

Against Cotton-Eyed Pranksters, Tsareena's Queenly Majesty completely neutralizes opposing Prankster status moves from Whimsicott and Grimmsnarl as well as priority Fake Out and Extreme Speed. Dual Wide Guard on Pelipper and Garganacl shuts down Gholdengo's Make It Rain, Sinistcha's Matcha Gotcha, and Arcanine's Heat Wave/Rock Slide. Under Pelipper's Damp Rock Rain, Mega Swampert and Archaludon outspeed and demolish Gholdengo, Arcanine, and Grimmsnarl, while Garganacl's Purifying Salt halves Ghost damage from Gholdengo and Sinistcha and melts Steel/Water types with 25% per-turn Salt Cure chip.

Mega Charizard Y plus Chlorophyll Venusaur is the primary mode: sun suppresses the opponent’s Water core while Venusaur immediately outspeeds and threatens Greninja, Gyarados, Toxapex, and Mamoswine. Raichu supplies Fake Out, Electroweb, and Gyarados pressure, while Tauros and Sableye disrupt the physical and Trick Room modes. Kingambit is reserved to pressure Reuniclus, Skeledirge, and Mega Metagross once Charizard has forced chip.

Against Fairy Tails, our Rain Offense engine combined with Queenly Majesty and Trick Room control completely shuts down their key win conditions. Mega Swampert under Drizzle rain outruns their entire team and picks up massive OHKOs with Wave Crash and 4x Ice Punch into Garchomp and Serperior. Tsareena's Queenly Majesty completely nullifies Talonflame's Gale Wings priority attacks and Sucker Punch while Pelipper provides Wide Guard against Garchomp's Earthquake and Rotom-W's Discharge. Archaludon abuses instant Electro Shot in rain, Draco Meteor, and Flash Cannon to destroy Mega Floette, while Galarian Slowking and Mimikyu offer secondary Trick Room control and potent Poison STAB against Fairy/Grass threats.

Mega Charizard Y + Chlorophyll Venusaur is the primary pressure mode, with Sun forcing fast Sleep Powder and strong Fire/Grass coverage into their bulky Grass, Water, and Steel options. Kingambit is preserved for Mega Gardevoir and Farigiraf, while Raichu supplies Fake Out, Lightning Rod, and Encore disruption. Tauros and Dragonite give the roster an Intimidate pivot and a separate Tailwind mode, so the team is not wholly dependent on Sun speed.

Fairy Tails leans on Floette-Mega, Garchomp, Rotom-Wash, and Aegislash, with Talonflame/Serperior/Spiritomb/Overqwil as flex picks. I bring six that answer each: Weavile speed-clamps Garchomp and Serperior with 4x/2x Ice and revenge-KOs Gale Wings Talonflame via priority Ice Shard; Gardevoir-Mega's Pixilate Hyper Voice threatens OHKOs on Spiritomb, Garchomp, and Overqwil; Venusaur-Mega's Thick Fat + Giga Drain handles Rotom-Wash and Manectric while Sludge Bomb chunks Serperior; Incineroar gives Intimidate/Fake Out pivoting and is my Aegislash answer (Fire/Dark super-effective on it); Skarmory is the Fairy resist that walls Floette and sets Tailwind; Sneasler goes Unburden-fast to delete Absol and pressure Overqwil, with Night Slash to cover Ghosts that ignore Close Combat.

Sun is the opponent's entire identity — Charizard-Mega-Y's Drought boosts Fire Blast to OHKO range on Metagross-Mega (89.8-280% in sun) and Venusaur's Chlorophyll doubles its speed. The answer is Gyarados with Damp Rock Rain Dance to override sun for 8 turns: in rain, Metagross survives Fire Blast (28.9-92.9%), Gyarados takes negligible Fire damage (7.4-22.9%), and both Gyarados Stone Edge (101.6-235.3%, guaranteed OHKO) and Greninja Hydro Pump (102.7-226.1%, guaranteed OHKO) cleanly remove Charizard. Klefki provides Prankster Safeguard to block Venusaur Sleep Powder and Sableye Will-O-Wisp, plus Light Screen/Reflect for bulk. Snorlax (Thick Fat) and Toxapex (Water-typing) are secondary Fire resists that tank Charizard even in sun (17.2-30.3% and 27.4-45.9% respectively). Metagross-Mega Hammer Arm is a guaranteed OHKO on Kingambit (108.2-228.6%), and Ice Punch handles Dragonite after Multiscale is chipped. Toxapex Haze shuts down DD Dragonite and any setup.

The opponent's identity is dual Prankster (Whimsicott + Grimmsnarl) backed by Gholdengo's Good as Gold status immunity and fast physical attackers (Tauros, Arcanine). I bring six that cover all angles: Corviknight provides Tailwind speed control and Mirror Armor to reflect their two Intimidate users back at them, Gyarados adds a second Intimidate plus Taunt and Lum Berry to absorb Prankster Thunder Wave, Metagross-Mega at 178 Spe speed-ties Tauros and hits Gholdengo with Earthquake while Meteor Mash threatens both Fairies, Snorlax is a Ghost-immune special wall that tanks Gholdengo and Thick Fats Arcanine, Skeledirge's Unaware shuts down any setup attempts, and Toxapex walls Milotic while landing a 4x SE Sludge Bomb on Whimsicott and providing Haze insurance.

The Drought Dodgers revolve around Charizard-Mega-Y's sun with Chlorophyll Venusaur, backed by Kingambit, Dragonite, Raichu, and Prankster Sableye. I answer Charizard with layered pressure: Sneasler's 4x Rock Slide (Life Orb, likely OHKO), Venusaur-Mega's Thick Fat tanking its sun Fire, and Incineroar resisting Fire entirely. Weavile (Focus Sash) outspeeds even sun Venusaur and OHKOs Dragonite through Multiscale, while Gardevoir's Pixilate Fairy nukes Dragonite/Sableye. Sneasler and Skarmory's Body Press crush Kingambit (I avoid Intimidating it due to Defiant), and Skarmory's Tailwind gives my slower mons speed control. I keep Skarmory and Gardevoir away from Charizard's sun Fire.

Heel Turn leans on an Incineroar + Farigiraf + Mega Gardevoir core with Sneasler or Weavile as fast physical pressure. Aegislash hard-walls Mega Gardevoir — immune to Focus Blast and Psychic, resists Pixilate Hyper Voice, and Wide Guard erases it for both my Pokémon — while Overqwil Intimidates the physical trio, OHKOs Gardevoir with Poison Jab, and Taunts Farigiraf's support. Rotom-Wash (immune to Fake Out and Close Combat) and Garchomp's Earthquake break Incineroar, Talonflame outruns Weavile by a point of Speed to Flare Blitz it and brings Tailwind, and Mega Floette is the late-game cleaner and guaranteed Sneasler answer.

Golden Gate runs the Pelipper + Swift Swim Mega Swampert rain core behind Archaludon and Tailwind Galarian Slowking, so I'm bringing the rain-hate six from my prep. Lead Serperior + Talonflame: Tailwind flips the Swift Swim speed edge, and Focus Sash Serperior survives one rain hit to Leaf Storm Swampert (verified OHKO, 100.5%+).
